items.stem: How did the Business class relate itself to the Civil Disobedience Movement? Explain with examples.
items.answer: Indian merchants and industrialists were eager to expand their businesses and reacted sharply against colonial policies that restricted their trading activity. They wanted protection against imports of foreign goods and a rupee–sterling exchange ratio that would discourage imports. To organise their interests they formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress in 1920 and the Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI) in 1927. Led by prominent industrialists such as Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla, they attacked colonial control over the Indian economy and supported the Civil Disobedience Movement, giving financial assistance and refusing to buy or sell imported goods. Most businessmen wanted trade to flourish without constraints, and so they saw swaraj as the condition for their own prosperity and backed the movement.

items.stem: Highlight the reasons for the growth of nationalist tensions in the Balkan region before the First World War.
items.answer: The Balkans was a region of great geographical and ethnic variation, comprising modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, whose inhabitants were broadly known as the Slavs. The spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism, together with the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire, made the region explosive; through the nineteenth century the Ottoman Empire tried to strengthen itself through modernisation and internal reforms but with little success. As the different Slavic nationalities struggled to define their identity and win independence, each claiming territory on the basis of past glory, the Balkans became an area of intense conflict. Alongside this, each of the big powers — Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary — was keen on countering the hold of the others over the Balkans and on extending its own control there. This rivalry led to a series of wars in the region and finally to the First World War.
items.concept: Impact of the First World War
items.ocr: This is a Nationalism-in-Europe question printed inside the Nationalism in India chapter; no Balkan concept exists in the chapter concept list, so the nearest available concept (Impact of the First World War) was cited.

items.stem:
The Civil Disobedience Movement saw the participation of different social classes and groups. Give reasons for the participation of the following:
(1) rich peasants
(2) poor peasants
(3) business classes
(4) industrial working classes
(5) women.
items.answer: Rich peasants: communities such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh joined because, as producers of commercial crops, they were hard hit by the trade depression and falling prices, and the government's refusal to reduce the revenue demand made them fight against high revenues. Poor peasants: they joined because they found it difficult to pay rent and wanted their unpaid rent to the landlord to be remitted. Business class: they reacted against colonial policies that restricted their activity, wanted protection against imports of foreign goods, and believed swaraj would cancel colonial restrictions so that trade could flourish freely. Industrial working class: they did not participate in large numbers except in the Nagpur region; some workers selectively adopted parts of the Gandhian programme, such as the boycott of foreign goods, as part of their own struggles against low wages and poor working conditions. Women: they took part on a large scale, joining protest marches, manufacturing salt and picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops, and many went to jail. Thus each group joined the movement for reasons rooted in its own grievances against colonial rule.

items.stem: The middle classes played an important role in the Non-Cooperation Movement in the cities. Explain. Why do you think that the movement slowed down in the cities?
items.answer: The middle classes led the movement in the cities. Thousands of students left government-controlled schools and colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, and lawyers gave up their legal practices. Council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras. Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires. The movement nevertheless slowed down in the cities for several reasons. Khadi cloth was more expensive than mass-produced mill cloth, so poor people could not afford it and could not boycott mill cloth for long. Boycotting British institutions also created a problem because there were no alternative national institutions to meet educational and legal needs. As a result students and teachers began trickling back to government schools and lawyers returned to work in government courts, and the urban phase of the movement gradually lost its momentum.

items.stem: How did Non-Cooperation movement start with participation of middle class people in the cities? Explain its impact on the economic front.
items.answer: The Non-Cooperation Movement began in the cities with the middle classes. It was launched by Gandhiji in 1920 to express resentment against actions considered oppressive, such as the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the Rowlatt Act, and thousands of students left government-controlled schools and colleges. Teachers and headmasters resigned and lawyers gave up their legal practices. Council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras, where the Justice Party, the party of non-Brahmans, felt that entering the council was one way of gaining power. On the economic front the effects were sharp: foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires. In many places traders and merchants refused to trade in foreign goods and even refused to finance foreign trade, so that the import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922. As the boycott spread, people used only Indian cloth and discarded foreign clothes, and the production of Indian textile mills and handloom went up greatly.

items.stem: Why did Gandhiji start Non-Cooperation Movement? Explain.
items.answer: Gandhiji started the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1921 for several reasons. He argued that British rule had been established in India with the cooperation of Indians and had survived only because of that cooperation, so the time had come to withdraw cooperation from the British. After returning from Africa in 1915 he had launched local satyagrahas, but he was looking for an opportunity to begin a national-level movement against the British. The First World War added greatly to the misery of the Indian people, as heavy taxes, high prices, famines and epidemics made life wretched. The British passed the Rowlatt Act despite the opposition of Indian leaders; the Act curbed political activity and allowed the detention of political prisoners. Finally, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the injustice done to Punjab made Indians angry and demanded redress. For these reasons Gandhiji launched the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem: Why was Congress reluctant to allow women to hold any position of authority within the organisation? How did women participate in Civil Disobedience Movement? Explain.
items.answer: Gandhiji was convinced that it was the duty of a woman to look after her home and family and that women should be good mothers and good wives, and for a long time the Congress was therefore reluctant to allow women to hold any position of authority within the organisation; it was content with a symbolic presence of women. Women nevertheless participated in the Civil Disobedience Movement in large numbers. During Gandhiji's Salt March thousands of women came out of their houses to listen to him. They joined protest marches, manufactured salt and picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops. Many were arrested and sent to jail. In urban areas these women came from high-caste families — for example Sarojini Naidu, Satyavati Devi and Kamla Nehru — while in rural areas they came from rich peasant households. Women broke open the doors of shops, came out on the roads and helped the movement's leaders. In Bombay a large section of Gujarati women, influenced by Gandhiji's idealism, took part in the national movement, and Bengal, the nerve centre of female education in India, saw increased participation, with women rallying before Bethune College, Calcutta in 1930 in support of the movement.

items.stem: Why did Gandhi decide to launch a nationwide ‘Satyagraha’ against the proposed Rowlatt Act (1919)? How was it opposed? Explain.
items.answer: The Rowlatt Act was passed in spite of the united opposition of the Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council. It gave the government enormous powers to suppress political agitation and allowed the detention of political prisoners without trial for two years, with no provision for appeal. The passing of such an unjust law aroused large-scale indignation, and Gandhiji, who had already formed a Satyagraha Sabha, therefore decided to call for a country-wide protest against it. Throughout the country 6 April 1919 was observed as a National Humiliation Day. Gandhiji wanted non-violent civil disobedience against such unjust laws, so hartals and rallies were organised in various cities, workers went on strike in railway workshops and shops were closed down. Communication, railway and telegraph lines were disrupted. The movement remained non-violent yet proved highly effective in opposing the Act.

items.stem: Why was the ‘Salt March’ considered an effective symbol of resistance against colonialism? Explain.
items.answer: Mahatma Gandhi found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the whole nation. On 31 January 1930 he sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands, one of which was the abolition of the salt tax. Salt was one of the most essential food items, consumed by rich and poor alike, and the tax on it together with the government monopoly over its production was regarded as an oppression on the people. Gandhiji's letter was an ultimatum: if his demands were not met by 11 March he would launch a civil disobedience campaign. When no reply came, he began his famous Salt March with 78 trusted volunteers, walking over 240 miles from his ashram at Sabarmati to the Gujarati coastal town of Dandi. The volunteers marched for 24 days, about 10 miles a day, and thousands came to hear Gandhiji wherever he stopped, where he explained what he meant by swaraj and urged people to peacefully defy the British. On 6 April he reached Dandi and ceremonially violated the law by manufacturing salt from sea water, and this act, which touched every Indian household, marked the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement and made the Salt March an effective symbol of resistance against colonialism.

items.stem: How did the Non-Cooperation Movement spread to the countryside and drew into its fold the struggles of peasants and tribal communities? Elaborate.
items.answer: From the cities the Non-Cooperation Movement spread into the countryside and drew the struggles of peasants and tribals into its fold. In Awadh the peasants' movement was led by Baba Ramchandra against talukdars and landlords who demanded extremely high rents and a variety of other cesses, and who forced peasants to work on their farms without any payment (begar). Peasants had no security of tenure and were regularly evicted so that they could acquire no right over the leased land; their demands were a reduction of revenue, the abolition of begar and a social boycott of oppressive landlords. In 1920 Jawaharlal Nehru began talking to the villagers and the Oudh Kisan Sabha was formed, and within a month 300 branches had been set up in the villages. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh a militant guerrilla movement spread in the early 1920s against the closure of forest areas by the colonial government, which prevented tribal people from entering the forests to graze cattle or collect fuelwood and fruits; they felt that their traditional rights were being denied. When the government forced them to contribute begar for road building, the hill people revolted. Their leader Alluri Sitaram Raju, inspired by Mahatma Gandhi, persuaded people to wear khadi and give up drinking, though he asserted that India could be liberated only by the use of force. In this way the movement acquired a rural and tribal dimension.

items.stem: How had the ‘First World War’ created economic problems in India? Explain with examples.
items.answer: The First World War created serious economic problems in India. It led to a huge increase in defence expenditure, which was financed by raising taxes and increasing custom duties. During the war years crop failure resulted in an acute shortage of food. Food prices rose sharply, almost doubling between 1913 and 1918, which increased the hardships of the people. Villages were called upon to supply soldiers, and in some rural areas the colonial government forced people to join the army, causing widespread resentment and anger and setting the stage for depression. On top of this an influenza epidemic spread and added to the hardships of the people, while the war weakened the gold standard. Thus the war brought high prices, scarcity, forced recruitment and disease, creating deep economic distress in India.

items.stem: “The Civil Disobedience Movement was different from the Non-co-operation Movement.” Support the statement with examples.
items.answer: The Civil Disobedience Movement was a movement of open defiance of British law, launched by Mahatma Gandhi in April 1930, and it differed from the Non-Cooperation Movement in several ways. It was a unique movement because Gandhiji found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation against the government monopoly over its production; the issue of salt looked ordinary at first but proved the most stirring one. In the Non-Cooperation Movement people were asked only to refuse cooperation with the British, whereas in the Civil Disobedience Movement they were asked not merely to deny cooperation but also to break colonial laws. The movement spread like wildfire and re-energised all classes of the nation: the salt law was broken, foreign cloth was boycotted, liquor shops were picketed, and peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes. Another important feature was the large-scale participation of women; thousands of women came out of their homes, joined protest marches, manufactured salt and picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops. These features show that the Civil Disobedience Movement went well beyond the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem: Why did Mahatma Gandhi find in ‘salt’ a powerful symbol that could unite the nation? Explain.
items.answer: Salt was a commodity consumed by every individual, rich and poor alike, and its stock in the seas and oceans was undepleting, so it was a gross atrocity on the part of the British Government to impose a tax on it and take its production under a state monopoly. Salt therefore offered an excellent opportunity to expose the malafide intention of the foreign government before the masses of India. Acting on this, Gandhiji sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands. The demands were wide ranging, some general and some specific, and concerned the interests of all sections of Indian society; the removal of the tax on salt was one of them. He specifically stated that if the Government appeared unwilling to negotiate on the demands by 11 March, the Congress would launch a civil disobedience campaign. As the British government gave no response, Gandhi launched the Dandi March, a 375 km march from Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal town of Dandi in Gujarat. On these counts salt became an effective symbol of resistance against colonialism, gathering nationwide support of the Indian masses and openly challenging British laws.
items.ocr: The book prints the Dandi March as beginning on 13th March 1930 and as a 375 km march; both figures are reproduced from the printed solution although other questions in the same chapter print 12 March and 240 miles.

items.stem: How did the Civil Disobedience Movement come into force in various parts of the country? Explain with examples.
items.answer: The Civil Disobedience Movement drew in different groups across the country, each for its own reasons. In the countryside the rich peasants of Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh were active in the movement; badly hit by the trade depression and falling prices, they became enthusiastic supporters. Many of the poor peasants were small tenants cultivating land rented from landlords, and as the depression continued they found it difficult to pay their rent, so they joined a variety of radical movements, often led by socialists and communists. The business classes reacted against colonial policies during the movement; wanting protection against imports of foreign goods, they supported the movement and refused to buy or sell imported goods. The movement also witnessed the large-scale participation of women, who came out of their homes, joined protest marches and picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops, and many of them went to jail. The plantation workers in Assam defied the authorities, left the plantations and headed home, believing that Gandhi Raj was near and that everyone would be given land in their own villages. In this way the movement came into force in different regions and among different social groups across India.

items.stem: Why was the Non-Cooperation Movement launched in 1920? Why did Gandhiji call off the movement in 1922?
items.answer: The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) was launched for several causes. There was a breach of trust committed by the British Government after the First World War, the enforcement of the Rowlatt Act, the unruly killing of peaceful demonstrators at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar in Punjab, and the so-called biased reforms effected through the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms. Dyarchy was introduced in the Bengal province under those same reforms. The dismemberment of the Ottoman Empire in Turkey, with the Khalifa disowned, angered Indian Muslims and brought the Khilafat cause into the movement. The movement came to a sudden halt in 1922. Things went out of hand when the police at Chauri-Chaura in the Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh fired at Congress volunteers and the infuriated mob, in retaliation, set the police station on fire and killed 22 policemen. Because the movement had turned violent, Gandhiji immediately suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem: Describe the Peasant Rebellion in Awadh during the Non-Cooperation Movement.
items.answer: The peasants of Awadh during the movement were led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier worked in Fiji as an indentured labourer. The peasants' movement was started to demand a reduction of revenue, the abolition of begar and a social boycott of oppressive landlords. During the movement Nai-Dhobi bandhs were organised at many places, so as to deprive the landlords even of the services of washermen and barbers. The movement was directed against the taluqdars and landlords who charged high revenue from the peasants. In 1920 Jawaharlal Nehru formed the Oudh Kisan Sabha to help the peasants free themselves from the clutches of the landlords, and within a month 300 branches had been set up in the villages. The movement spread quickly, and in 1921 the houses of taluqdars and merchants were attacked, bazaars were looted and grain hoards were taken over. Thus the Awadh peasant rebellion became a militant rural wing of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.stem:
How did Gandhiji bring the masses into the National Movement?
or
How as the freedom struggle for India’s independence was converted into a Mass movement by M. K. Gandhi?
items.answer: Gandhiji's simple, saintly life and his habit of convincing the masses in their local languages made him extremely popular as a leader. His undisputed leadership and magnetic personality helped to coordinate and unite the movement. His policy of non-violent satyagraha brought millions into the struggle; the Champaran satyagraha, for instance, brought the peasants in. He launched three powerful mass movements — Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India — which influenced millions of Indians of every section of society to show bravery, self-confidence and revolutionary passive resistance against British rule. His new methods of agitation, such as hartals, boycott, civil disobedience and non-payment of taxes, appealed to ordinary people. Under his guidance Indians withstood brutal repression and willingly accepted imprisonment, lathi charges and bullets for the sake of freedom. Through his programmes of social reform, the charkha, cottage industries and his fight against untouchability, the Harijans and depressed classes joined the freedom struggle and millions gained employment. His deep commitment to Hindu-Muslim unity and his secular ideals persuaded every community to unite for the noble cause of freedom. His support to the Ahmedabad mill workers' strike in 1918 and his satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act kept him in close touch with the masses, and he became the Father of the Nation. He was the first Indian nationalist leader who identified his life and manner of living with that of the common people and earned the title of ‘Mahatma’. In these ways Gandhiji converted the freedom struggle into a genuine mass movement.
